The 1930s two-color Technicolor process musical revue King of Jazz was recently released in the Criterion Collection, and I just finished watching it. I decided to come here to say that it's worth a look. It offers a fascinating snapshot glance into the culture of the period, which was the very beginning of the Great Depression, when the boozy, heady glow of the Roaring Twenties was still lingering like a gin hangover.

I found the film entertaining, although it is of uneven quality. Some of the musical and dance numbers are delightful, while other's tend to drone on like an out-of-tune cello. Some of the very brief dramatic numbers are funny, other's not so much.

One interesting oddity -- although the film is titled King of Jazz it contains no jazz, at least as we would recognize it today. The Paul Whiteman Orchestra is, frankly, second rate. It includes a banjo player, an acoustic guitar player, a piccolo player -- why, I have no idea. I think that if Benny Goodman ever watched this movie, he must have left the theater shaking his head.

Numbers that stand out are the brief Negro savage drum dance at the opening of Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue, Bing Crosby and two nobodies singing "Happy Feet," and an incredibly flexible lady contortionist doing an Apache woman-abuse dance. The Apache Dance (as it was called -- it was also known as the Tough Dance and La Danse Apache) involved a man slapping a woman around on stage. It is highly politically incorrect for today's viewer. So is the Negro drum dance, for that matter. But both are great dance numbers. Also worthy of note are the appearances of "Rubber Legs" Al Norman. He could have given Fred Astaire an idea or two.

Anyway, I highly recommend that you download this movie from Pirate Bay and give it a watch, if you have any interest in 1930s dance revue movies such as those produced by Busby Berkeley.
